issues.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption over immovable property does not accrue from a contract for sale when the governing transfer law requires a registered instrument to transfer ownership.
material_facts: The pre-emption suit was filed on the basis of agreements for sale before a sale deed had been executed.
The agreements for sale did not themselves create an interest in the property or transfer proprietary title.
The sale deed was executed after the suit was filed.
issues.conclusion: No enforceable right of pre-emption had accrued when the suit was filed on the basis of the agreements for sale; the later sale deed could not validate that claim as pleaded.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, a contract for sale does not of itself create an interest in or charge on immovable property, and a transfer of ownership of the relevant kind must be made by a registered instrument. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act support the requirement that a document requiring registration cannot affect the property unless registered. The statutory pre-emption rights under sections 176 to 178 and 183 of the Berar Land Revenue Code do not broaden the meaning of sale beyond the applicable transfer law, and Mohammedan or other personal law cannot override that law. The Court relied on Immudipattam Thirugnana S. O. Kondema Naik v. Peria Dorasami, Sitaram Bhaurao Deshmukh v. Jiaul Hasan Sirajul Khan, Begum v. Mohammad Yakub, and the reasoning of Mahmood, J., in Janki v. Girjadat.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_suit and transfer_requires_registered_instrument and suit_filed_before_registered_transfer and claim_based_on_contract_for_sale

predicates.preemption_enforcement_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding to enforce a claimed right to take the place of a property purchaser.
predicates.transfer_requires_registered_instrument: The applicable transfer law requires ownership of property of this kind to be transferred by a registered instrument.
predicates.suit_filed_before_registered_transfer: The claimant filed the proceeding before the ownership transfer was completed by the required instrument.
predicates.claim_based_on_contract_for_sale: The claimant relied on an agreement for sale that had not itself transferred ownership.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks pre-emption based on a contract for sale before the required registered transfer is completed, the claimed right has not accrued at the time of filing.

issues.legal_issue: Using lawful means to avoid the accrual of a right of pre-emption is not, without more, fraud against the pre-emptor.
material_facts: The parties arranged for the land to be diverted to non-agricultural use before executing the sale deed.
The pre-emption suit was filed while the transaction remained incomplete and before the sale deed was executed.
The claim was based on earlier agreements for sale, not on the later sale deed.
issues.conclusion: It was neither illegal nor fraudulent for the parties to use legitimate means to avoid a claim of pre-emption, and the pre-emptor had no equity requiring the Court to assist the claim.
issues.legal_principle: A right of pre-emption is a weak statutory right, not viewed with favour, and may be defeated by legitimate methods. The Court relied on Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh, which recognized that the right may be defeated by legitimate methods, and held that lawful steps to avoid pre-emption are not fraud. The Court also stated that conduct before completion of a pre-emptible transfer could not ordinarily be treated as fraud to deprive a pre-emptor of the right.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_suit and parties_used_steps_to_avoid_preemption and steps_were_lawful and no_preemptible_transfer_completed_at_filing

predicates.preemption_enforcement_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding to enforce a claimed right to take the place of a property purchaser.
predicates.parties_used_steps_to_avoid_preemption: The parties to a proposed property transaction took steps intended to prevent a right of pre-emption from arising.
predicates.steps_were_lawful: The steps taken by the parties were lawful means of arranging or completing the transaction.
predicates.no_preemptible_transfer_completed_at_fil: No transaction that could be pre-empted had been completed when the claimant filed the proceeding.

issues.definition: When parties use lawful steps to avoid pre-emption and no pre-emptible transfer has been completed when the proceeding is filed, those steps do not amount to fraud.
